The C++ and DSA internship in short

In the SkillMe C++ and DSA internship you build one of 3 projects, such as AlgoCore: A Command-Line Data Toolkit, a project where you build a small C++ command-line tool that stores and searches records, learning core language features and the STL along the way. In week 1 you write a C++ program that stores a list of student records in memory and lets you add and print them from a text menu. By week 4 you finish the project with a feature that ties everything together: importing many records at once from a CSV file, generating a summary report, and cleaning up the codebase for a strong final demo. Each milestone is posted on LinkedIn and checked against that week's checklist before it counts. Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month.

What you build

One of 3 real projects, built over four weeks

You are assigned one of these projects when you start, and build it milestone by milestone.

AlgoCore: A Command-Line Data Toolkit

Build a small C++ command-line tool that stores and searches records, learning core language features and the STL along the way.

  1. W1Structs, Functions and a Console Menu
  2. W2Classes, File Saving and Sorting
  3. W3A Hand-Built Data Structure and Recursion
  4. W4Polish, Bulk Import and a Final Report

PixelForge: A Terminal 2D Game

Build a small ASCII/terminal-based 2D game in C++, adding movement, collisions and simple physics week by week.

  1. W1A Moving Character on a Grid
  2. W2Obstacles, Collisions and Classes
  3. W3Simple Physics: Gravity and Velocity
  4. W4Levels, Scoring and a Polished Demo

DataVault: A Simple In-Memory Database Engine

Build a tiny command-line database engine in C++ that stores records, indexes them for fast lookup, and supports simple queries.

  1. W1Records, Tables and Basic Commands
  2. W2Filtering, Updating and Deleting
  3. W3Indexing for Fast Lookup
  4. W4Multiple Tables, Tests and a Final Demo
Week by week

What each week of the C++ and DSA internship covers

Shown for AlgoCore: A Command-Line Data Toolkit. The other projects follow the same four-week shape.

  1. Week 1 of 4

    Structs, Functions and a Console Menu

    Beginner2-3 hours

    Write a C++ program that stores a list of student records in memory and lets you add and print them from a text menu. This gets your toolchain working and practises the basics every later week builds on.

    What you learn

    • Compiling and running a C++ program from the terminal (g++)
    • struct to group related data together
    • std::vector to store a growing list of records
    • Passing data by reference (&) to avoid copies
    • A simple menu loop with switch and std::cin

    What you submit

    • main.cpp with a Student struct and a working add/list/quit menu
    • Input validation that survives bad input without crashing
    • A README with build and run instructions
    • A short terminal recording or screenshots showing the menu in use
    How week 1 is reviewed
    • The program compiles with -Wall -Wextra and shows no warnings
    • Adding several students and choosing 'Show All' lists them correctly
    • Typing letters where a number is expected does not crash the program
    • Choosing Quit exits cleanly

    Stretch goal: Add a 'Show Top Scorer' menu option that finds the student with the highest marks.

  2. Week 2 of 4

    Classes, File Saving and Sorting

    Beginner+2-3 hours

    Turn your struct into a proper class with encapsulated data, save and load records to a file so nothing is lost between runs, and add search and sort features using the STL.

    What you learn

    • Classes with private members, constructors and getter methods
    • Reading and writing plain text files with std::ifstream / std::ofstream
    • std::sort with a custom comparator (lambda)
    • Linear search with std::find_if
    • Splitting code into a .h header and .cpp source file

    What you submit

    • A Student class in its own header/source files with encapsulated data
    • Save/load to a text file so data survives between runs
    • Sort-by-marks and search-by-name menu options
    • An updated README describing the saved file format
    How week 2 is reviewed
    • Adding students, quitting, and restarting the program shows the same data
    • Sort by Marks lists students highest-to-lowest correctly
    • Search by Name finds a student even with partial or different-case input handled sensibly
    • The program still runs cleanly if the save file is missing

    Stretch goal: Support multiple save 'profiles' by asking for a filename at startup instead of hardcoding one.

  3. Week 3 of 4

    A Hand-Built Data Structure and Recursion

    Intermediate2-3 hours

    Add a feature that needs a data structure or algorithm you implement yourself, not just an STL call, so you understand what's happening underneath. You'll add a simple linked-list based history log and a recursive search or sort.

    What you learn

    • Implementing a singly linked list from scratch (nodes and pointers)
    • Recursion, using it to implement binary search or merge sort by hand
    • Time complexity basics (why binary search is O(log n) vs linear O(n))
    • Smart pointers (std::unique_ptr) as a safer alternative to raw new/delete
    • Basic exception handling with try/catch

    What you submit

    • A hand-built singly linked list tracking an action history
    • A hand-written binary search (or merge sort) used somewhere in the app
    • try/catch error handling around file operations
    • A short written comparison of binary search vs linear search timing
    How week 3 is reviewed
    • Show History correctly lists actions in the order they happened
    • Your binary search returns the same result as a linear search on the same sorted data
    • Deliberately breaking the save file (or removing write permission) shows a friendly message instead of a crash
    • No raw new without a matching delete or a smart pointer remains in the code

    Stretch goal: Add an 'Undo last action' feature that pops the most recent entry off your history and reverses it.

  4. Week 4 of 4

    Polish, Bulk Import and a Final Report

    Intermediate+2-3 hours

    Finish the project with a feature that ties everything together: importing many records at once from a CSV file, generating a summary report, and cleaning up the codebase for a strong final demo.

    What you learn

    • Reading and parsing a CSV file with std::stringstream
    • Generating a formatted text report (averages, min/max, grade distribution)
    • Basic unit testing by writing small standalone test functions
    • Code cleanup: consistent naming, removing dead code, adding comments

    What you submit

    • CSV bulk import with a summary of successes/skipped rows
    • A 'Generate Report' feature with averages and grade distribution
    • At least 4 small self-checking test functions runnable via a --test flag
    • A polished README with build/run/test instructions and screenshots
    How week 4 is reviewed
    • Importing a CSV with a few deliberately bad rows still loads the good ones and reports the bad ones
    • The generated report's average matches a manual calculation on the same data
    • Running with --test prints PASS for every test function
    • The code compiles warning-free and has no leftover debug prints or dead code

    Stretch goal: Export the generated report to a .txt or .csv file instead of only printing it to the terminal.

C++ and DSA internship: questions and answers

What will I build in the C++ and DSA internship?

You are assigned one of 3 projects: AlgoCore: A Command-Line Data Toolkit, PixelForge: A Terminal 2D Game or DataVault: A Simple In-Memory Database Engine. Each is a single project built up over four weekly milestones, so each week adds to the last.

What skills will I learn in the C++ and DSA internship?

The C++ and DSA internship works with C++20, DSA and Problem Solving. Week 1: compiling and running a C++ program from the terminal (g++); struct to group related data together. Week 2: classes with private members, constructors and getter methods; reading and writing plain text files with std::ifstream / std::ofstream. Week 3: implementing a singly linked list from scratch (nodes and pointers); recursion, using it to implement binary search or merge sort by hand. Week 4: reading and parsing a CSV file with std::stringstream; generating a formatted text report (averages, min/max, grade distribution).

Do I need experience to apply for the C++ and DSA internship?

You need the basics of C++20, DSA and Problem Solving, not prior internship experience. Week 1 starts at beginner level, where you write a C++ program that stores a list of student records in memory and lets you add and print them from a text menu. Week 4 reaches intermediate+ level. A short screening quiz (8 questions, about 5 minutes) checks you are ready to start.

How is each C++ and DSA milestone reviewed?

Every week has a checklist, and a milestone is approved only when it meets all of it. For week 1 of AlgoCore: A Command-Line Data Toolkit, that means: the program compiles with -Wall -Wextra and shows no warnings; adding several students and choosing 'Show All' lists them correctly; typing letters where a number is expected does not crash the program; choosing Quit exits cleanly. Reviewers include engineers who work at Walmart, Google and LinkedIn, and work that misses the bar comes back with notes.

What can I put on my resume after the C++ and DSA internship?

Each approved milestone gives you a line you can back up with a public LinkedIn post: Built a C++ command-line tool using structs and std::vector to manage records; Wrote input validation that keeps the program running on bad input; Compiled clean with -Wall -Wextra and no warnings; Refactored a C++ CLI tool into a proper class with file-based persistence; Implemented sorting and searching using the STL (std::sort, std::find_if, lambdas); Split code across header and source files for a cleaner project structure; Implemented a linked list and binary search from scratch in C++; Added error handling with try/catch and replaced raw pointers with smart pointers; Measured and compared binary search vs linear search performance; Added CSV bulk import and an automated summary report to a C++ CLI tool; Wrote self-checking test functions to verify core logic; Polished and documented a 4-week C++ project from scratch to a working demo.

What are the other projects in the C++ and DSA internship?

PixelForge: A Terminal 2D Game: Build a small ASCII/terminal-based 2D game in C++, adding movement, collisions and simple physics week by week. DataVault: A Simple In-Memory Database Engine: Build a tiny command-line database engine in C++ that stores records, indexes them for fast lookup, and supports simple queries. Every project follows the same four-week shape, with one reviewed milestone a week.

Is the C++ and DSA internship paid? Is there a stipend?

Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month. It is performance-based and goes to the interns whose reviewed C++ and DSA work stands out in their cohort, not to every intern.

How much time does it take?

4 weeks, one milestone a week, each planned for about 2-3 hours. It is fully remote and open worldwide, so you work around college or a job.
